releases.title: Fix — Android builds failed at signing since v1.10.0
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.11.0 is unchanged. **No screen, field, module or behaviour has been removed, renamed or moved.** This release changes two build scripts and one workflow step. Nothing in the platform, the web app or the phone app's own code is touched.

## Update / Modifications

### Fixed: `Could not get unknown property 'MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE'`

**This was introduced by v1.10.0 and it was my mistake.** Android builds would have failed at the Gradle step, about seventy seconds in, from v1.10.0 onward.

**What actually happened.** The workflow wrote the four signing values into `android/gradle.properties` by appending them with the shell:

```
{ echo "MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE=release.jks"; … } >> android/gradle.properties
```

That is correct only while the file already ends in a newline. `expo prebuild` writes that file, and what it ends with depends on which config plugins are installed. **v1.10.0 added `expo-build-properties`** — to set the Android API level for Play — and with it installed the last line became `android.extraMavenRepos=[]` **with no trailing newline**. So the append produced:

```
android.extraMavenRepos=[]MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE=release.jks
MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS=cvskey
MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD=…
MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD=…
```

Gradle saw `android.extraMavenRepos` with a strange value and **no `MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE` at all**. The other three were on their own lines and were perfectly fine — which is exactly why the error named only the first one, and why it read as a mystery rather than as a missing file.

**How it was found.** Rather than guessing, `expo prebuild` was run here against the real project, with and without `expo-build-properties`:

- without it, the file ends `android.useLegacyPackaging=false` **with** a newline — which is why every build up to v1.9.x worked;
- with it, the file ends `android.extraMavenRepos=[]` **without** one.

The old append was then run against that real file and reproduced the failure exactly: `MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE` came back undefined while `MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS` came back correct — the precise shape of the error you saw.

**The fix.** The properties are no longer appended. A new script reads the file, replaces those four keys, writes it back, and then **reads it again to check Gradle will really find all four**, failing in a second with a plain message if not — rather than twenty minutes later inside Gradle. It also means running it twice replaces rather than duplicates a key, handles a value containing `=` (a password often does), and strips Windows line endings that would otherwise leave a carriage return inside a password.

### The Gradle file now explains itself if this ever recurs

The generated signing block used a bare `MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE`. When that is not defined, Groovy's error is *"Could not get unknown property … for SigningConfig$AgpDecorated_Decorated{…}"*, which tells nobody what to do.

It now reads the property defensively and, if it is missing, stops with a sentence saying which property it is, which workflow step is supposed to write it, and what it means if that step did not run.

## Performance

Unchanged. The new script is one file read and one write, replacing an append.

## Logs

Unchanged. The signing values are never printed — the script reports only the names of the keys it set, never their values.

## Verified

- `npm test` — **146 checks**, including **21 new ones** for this. The first of them is this exact failure, reproduced: a properties file ending `android.extraMavenRepos=[]` with no newline, which now resolves correctly and would have failed before.
- The whole sequence was run here against a **real `expo prebuild` output** — prebuild, write the properties, patch `build.gradle` — and all four properties come back correctly, with `android.extraMavenRepos` left intact on its own line.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean on both the platform and the app; `npm run build` clean; `npm run verify:bundle` bundles.

**Still not verifiable here:** this container has no Android SDK, so Gradle itself cannot be run. What has been proved is that the properties Gradle reads are now present and correct, which is the thing that was broken.

## Build repository

`mobile/` and `.github/` **must be pushed before the next Android build** — the fix is in `.github/scripts/`, so the platform alone does nothing. The revision markers were bumped to `1.11.1`; Mobile App Release will report the repository as behind until it is pushed.

releases.title: Chats on the phone, rebuilt as a proper messenger
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.10.0 is unchanged. **No screen, field, module or behaviour has been removed, renamed or moved.** Every existing conversation, group, notice, attachment, permission and build works exactly as before.

Specifically preserved in the app's Chats:

- **Every message already sent** renders as it always did; nothing was migrated.
- **Attachments** — sending, opening, Save, the 20 MB limit and the "Exceeded File Size" wording — unchanged.
- **New chat**, **New group** and the people picker — unchanged, same permissions.
- **The scrolling notice** at the top of the app — unchanged.
- **The web Chats page is untouched.** This release changes the phone only.
- **Polling fallback** still works when there is no real-time service; everything new degrades to it rather than depending on it.

## New Features

### The conversation now looks and behaves like a phone messenger

These are the conventions every messaging app has settled on, and they are now all here:

- **Bubbles with a tail**, drawn from borders so they take the bubble's own colour and stay sharp at any screen density.
- **The time inside the bubble**, tucked into the bottom-right corner rather than on its own line.
- **Ticks on your own messages** — ✓ when sent, **✓✓ in blue** once everyone in the conversation has read it, and a clock face while it is still going out.
- **Date separators** — *Today*, *Yesterday*, *Monday*, then a full date.
- **Consecutive messages grouped**. Three messages from one person in a minute form one block with one timestamp and one tail, instead of three identical-looking bubbles.
- **Sender names in colour** in groups, and the same person is always the same colour everywhere — the colour comes from their id, not their position in the list, which is the whole point of colouring them.
- **A jump-to-latest button** that appears only when you have scrolled away from the newest message.
- **"… is typing"**, sent at most once every three seconds (one request per keystroke would be absurd) and clearing itself four seconds after the last signal.
- **A rounded composer** with the attach button inside the field and a round Send button beside it.
- **The conversation sits on a tinted ground**, so bubbles read as cards on a surface.

**On colour:** the palette is **each company's own brand colour**, taken from the build — not anybody else's. This app is white-label, so a borrowed palette would be wrong for every company that is not that brand, and no other company's logo, artwork or assets are used anywhere in this.

### Messages appear the instant you send them

Your message now appears in the conversation immediately, carrying a clock face where its ticks will be, and is replaced by the real one when the server answers. On a weak signal that is the difference between an app that feels instant and one that appears to have swallowed what you typed. **If the send fails the placeholder is removed and your text goes back into the box**, so nothing is lost either way — the same guarantee as before, now visible.

### The conversation list reads at a glance

- **A tick on your own last message**, so you can see what has been read without opening anything.
- **"You:" or the sender's first name** in front of a group's last message.
- **Phone-style times** — a clock time today, *Yesterday*, then a short date.
- **An unread count** in the company's brand colour, with the time and preview emphasised while unread.
- **A search box** that filters what is already loaded — no request per keystroke.

## Update / Modifications

### Fixed: ticks could never have changed

Worth stating plainly, because it would have shipped as a feature that quietly never worked.

The app catches up by asking only for messages **newer** than the last one it holds. A read receipt arrives against a message that is already on screen, so under that scheme it could never arrive at all — a sent message would have shown one tick for the rest of its life.

Two things now carry it: the conversation subscribes to the **`message.read`** signal, which moves the ticks live; and where there is no real-time service, every sixth poll (about half a minute) the visible page is re-read and **only the read counts are merged in**, leaving scroll position untouched and moving no message. That second path is why this works on a weak connection rather than only on a good one.

### A small server change behind the list ticks

`lastMessage` on a conversation now also records **who sent it** (`byId`). Without that the list could only compare display names to guess whether the last message was yours, which breaks the moment two people share a first name. It is one additional field; nothing was changed or removed, and existing conversations simply gain it on their next message.

### Scroll no longer jumps while you are reading back

Arriving messages used to scroll the conversation to the bottom unconditionally. If you were reading something from last week, it yanked you away. **It now only follows the conversation when you are already at the newest message** — otherwise the jump button appears and the choice is yours.

## Performance

- Typing is announced at most once every three seconds, not once per keystroke.
- Search filters what is already loaded; it makes no requests.
- Read counts refresh over the real-time channel when it is available, costing nothing; the polling fallback adds **one request per half-minute** and only while a conversation is open.
- Grouping and date pills are computed in one pass over the messages already held.
- Ticks and date pills are memoised, so a new message does not re-render every bubble above it.

## Logs

Unchanged. Messages, attachments and read receipts are recorded exactly as before; none of the above adds or removes a record.

## Verified

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean on both the platform and the app.
- `npm test` — **125 checks**, including **32 new ones** covering message grouping, tick states, date pills and list times.
- `npm run build` clean.
- `npm run verify:bundle` — Metro bundles the app exactly as Gradle will.

**One thing this check earned its keep on:** the layout rules were first put in `shared/`, alongside the platform's other shared code. The bundle check refused it — the build repository receives only `mobile/` and `.github/`, so `shared/` is not there and the app would have failed to build after a twenty-minute wait. It now lives in `mobile/src/lib/`. This is the same class of failure as the v1.8.12 `netinfo` one, caught before a build rather than after.

**What could not be verified here:** this container has no Android or iOS emulator, so the preview sent with this release is a hand-built layout preview, not a device screenshot. The real rendering comes from the build.

## Build repository

`mobile/` and `.github/` must be pushed to the build repository with this release. The revision markers were bumped to `1.11.0`; Mobile App Release will report the repository as behind until it is pushed.

releases.title: Build controls, store credentials, group chat on the phone, and a tighter interface
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.9.0 is unchanged. **No screen, field, module or behaviour has been removed, renamed or moved.** Every existing user, role, permission, conversation, build, connector and setting works exactly as it did before this release.

Specifically preserved:

- **Every URL already printed, pasted or in a QR code keeps working.** The addresses shown for connectors now read as the company's own domain, but the old deployment address still answers — both reach the same application. Nothing in the field breaks.
- **The Staff / Customer switch stays.** You asked to remove it from the app; because removing it was the only way to create a Customer from a phone, it has been made compact instead, exactly as you chose. The web is untouched.
- **The Android build pipeline is unchanged for direct-install builds.** The same signing key, the same callback, the same S3 upload.
- **Cancelling a build still works** and still answers on the old address; "Stop" is the same action under a clearer name.
- **No screen moved in the interface pass.** Spacing, type size and corner radii changed; layout did not.

## New Features

### Watch a build, and pause or stop it

Super Admin → Company → **Mobile App** and → **Mobile App Release** now show any running build above the table, with a live bar, a percentage and the step it is on — *Waiting for a build machine*, *Installing the app's packages*, *Making the native project*, *Compiling and bundling*, *Uploading the finished app*. The figures are reported by the build itself as it passes each step, so they are a record of what happened rather than a timer pretending to be progress. The page now refreshes every 5 seconds while something is running, instead of every 20.

Three controls appear while a build is live, in both places: **Pause**, **Resume** and **Stop**. Stop asks to confirm first.

> **Please read this one.** GitHub Actions has no pause. A run is either going or cancelled; nothing can freeze a build machine mid-step and pick it up later. So **Pause cancels the run and remembers the version and build number, and Resume starts that same version again from the beginning.** The screen says exactly that under the bar — *"Resume starts it again (same version)"* — so nobody expects it to carry on from 60%. This is the same behaviour, and the same wording, as the FnB installer screens you sent. If you would rather Pause simply did not exist, say so and it comes out.
>
> Resume reuses the same row rather than creating a new one, so the history does not fill with half-builds, and a tester who was told to expect v1.0.0.17 still gets v1.0.0.17.

### App store credentials, and why the iOS button is grey

Mobile App Release has a new **App store credentials** panel, under *Start a build*. It lists three groups — **iOS signing**, **App Store Connect** and **Google Play** — and for each one: what it unlocks, where it comes from, which parts are already saved and which are missing. Files are uploaded directly; everything is sealed to the build repository's public key and stored as a repository secret. **Nothing is kept in this platform's database**, and GitHub never gives a secret's value back, so the panel can show that something is present but never what it is.

**The iOS button is no longer a dead grey button.** It now says why, on hover and in a banner: *"4 of 4 Apple credentials are missing. They cannot be generated here — they come from an Apple Developer Program membership."* Add them and **iOS switches itself on**, with nothing further to set.

This matters because of a trap that was already there: iOS previously needed `MOBILE_IOS_SIGNING=1` set by hand on the platform **as well as** the certificates in the repository. Somebody could have supplied every certificate correctly and still found the button grey, with nothing on screen explaining it. Having the credentials is now the condition.

**What is still needed from you, and cannot come from here:** an Apple Developer Program membership (99 USD/year), a distribution certificate (.p12 and its password), a provisioning profile, and an App Store Connect API key (.p8, Key ID, Issuer ID). The whole iOS pipeline — macOS runner, `pod install`, `xcodebuild` archive, export and upload to App Store Connect — is already written and waiting.

### Store compliance

- **iOS builds now run on `macos-15`.** This is a real defect found while checking: the workflow used `macos-14`, which carries Xcode 15, and **App Store Connect refuses a build made with an Xcode that old** — it would have failed at upload, after a twenty-minute build.
- **The Android API level is now set explicitly to 35** rather than left at Expo's default of 34, which Google Play no longer accepts for updates. It is a setting (`ANDROID_TARGET_SDK`), not a hard-coded number, because Play raises this bar every August and the day it moves is the day an upload starts being refused — raising it should not need a code change and a release.
- **The export-compliance answer is declared** (`ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption: false`), which is correct for an app that only speaks HTTPS and stops every App Store upload stalling on the same emailed question.

### Group chat from the phone

The app's Chats screen now has **New group** beside **New chat**: a name, a search, and tap the people to add. It appears only for someone whose role allows it — the same permission the web checks — so a tele-caller does not get a button that answers "not allowed". Names and roles only, as everywhere in chat.

### The app tells you when there is a newer version

A bar appears across the top of the app when a newer build exists: *"Version 1.0.0.17 is available — tap Update to download and install it."* It is checked when the app opens and each time it returns to the foreground. **A push notification also goes out the moment a build finishes**, to that company's phones that are not already on that version.

An Android app installed from an `.apk` has no store to update it, so without this a phone can sit on an old build indefinitely with nobody aware. Only installable builds are announced — a store build is an `.aab` or an App Store `.ipa`, which no phone installs directly. A version somebody dismisses stays dismissed until a newer one exists.

## Update / Modifications

### Fixed: QR code and campaign form URLs showed the platform's address

Under **Integration**, the endpoint URL and the hosted form URL were built from `APP_BASE_URL` — the Vercel deployment address — rather than the company's own. A QR code printed for a camp, or a form URL pasted into a campaign, is seen by the public and lives for months on a poster; it has to read as the company's own address.

They now use the company's **custom domain** if it has one, otherwise its **subdomain of the platform's base domain** (`credoone.mhw.credovation.tech`), falling back to the old behaviour only if neither is set. **Both addresses reach the same application, so this changes what is shown and copied, never where it goes — every URL already in the field keeps working.** The lookup is cached for a minute per company, so listing twenty connectors does not re-read the same two fields twenty times.

### Chat attachments can be downloaded

Every attachment now has a **download** control — a button on a file, and one that appears over an image on hover (a **Save** link on the phone). It fetches a separate link that saves the file **under its own name** rather than the random key it is stored as. The link for *viewing* deliberately does not carry that, so a picture can still be shown in place.

### The attachment limit is 20 MB, and says so in your words

Raised from 15 MB. A file over the limit is refused **before it is uploaded**, in the browser and on the phone, with the exact wording you asked for: **"Exceeded File Size"**, followed by the actual size and the limit. The server says the same if something reaches it. There is now a test asserting that exact phrase, so it cannot drift.

### A more compact interface

As agreed — **density and polish, with no layout changes**. Table rows, inputs and buttons each lose a few pixels of padding, the type scale is slightly tighter, corner radii are consistent, and focus rings are less heavy. On a table of twenty rows this is most of a screenful recovered. Every section is exactly where it was.

On the phone: one shared scale of four spacing steps, three radii and five type sizes, replacing a mix that made screens read as assembled rather than designed. Dashboard tiles now lead with the number rather than an upper-case caption; conversation rows and chat bubbles are tighter; the Staff/Customer switch is a compact inline control instead of a full-height section, which had been pushing **Save** off the bottom of a small screen.

### Also

- **Users** was added to the app's screen list in v1.9.0; it still has to be ticked under Super Admin → Company → Mobile App for a company whose screen list was already saved.
- A build that is paused is no longer flipped to "cancelled" by the run it just cancelled, which used to arrive a second later and take the Resume button away from a row somebody was still looking at.

## Performance

- The connector address is cached a minute per company — one read instead of one per connector per page.
- A running build is polled every 5 seconds and a paused one not at all; nothing changes about a paused build until somebody presses Resume.
- Progress is pushed by the build rather than polled from GitHub, so following a build costs no GitHub API calls at all.
- The app's update check is one small public request on launch and on returning to the foreground, and is skipped entirely when the platform does not answer.
- Attachment bytes never pass through the database; the upload streams to S3 and the message carries only a key.

## Logs

- Pause, Resume and Stop are each recorded with who did it, which company and which version.
- Opening and downloading an attachment are recorded separately, with the file's name.
- Saving store credentials is recorded by which credential names were written — never their values.

## Verified

releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.16 is unchanged. **No screen, field, module or behaviour has been removed, renamed or moved.** Every existing user, role, permission, conversation, build and setting works exactly as it did before this release.

Specifically preserved:

- **Users already created stay staff.** The new user type defaults to *Staff*, so every existing row reads as it always did and nothing had to be migrated.
- **Role Management works as before.** Roles, the permission grid, the plan caps and the per-user role assignment are untouched — this release only adds to the user form.
- **Existing chats are untouched.** Every message already sent is still a text message and still renders the same way.
- **The mobile build pipeline is unchanged.** Signing, the callback, the S3 upload and the revision markers all behave as in v1.8.16.

## New Features

### Customers can be given a sign-in, and tied to the record they already are

Under **Settings → Role Management → Users** (web) and the new **Users** screen in the app, a user can now be created as one of two types:

- **Staff** — somebody who works there. This is the default and what every existing user is.
- **Customer** — somebody who signs in to talk to you, rather than to work there.

A customer can optionally be **mapped to a client or a lead** through a dropdown that searches as it is typed. It matches on name, business name, phone, WhatsApp number, e-mail address or client code, says whether each hit is a *client* or a *lead*, and shows the mapped name back on the users list afterwards.

The mapping is **optional on purpose**: a customer who is not on the books yet still gets a sign-in and can still talk. And it is one field, not two — the platform works out from the record itself whether it is a client or a lead, so the wrong one cannot be filled in.

### Roles for users created in the app

The **Users** screen is new on the phone, and a role is required on it exactly as on the web. The list shows each person's type, role and whether they are disabled; tapping a row edits them, including their role, status and password.

This screen is governed by **Role Management › Users** permission *and* by the company's **Mobile Modules** — it appears in Super Admin → Company → Mobile App as a new tick box named **Users**. For a company whose screen list was already saved, it must be ticked before it appears in the app; a company with no explicit list gets it from whatever its modules allow.

### Attachments in chats

Both the web Chats page and the app's conversation screen now take a file:

- **Images, PDF, Word, Excel, CSV and plain text**, up to **15 MB** each.
- An image appears in the conversation; anything else opens in whatever already opens that kind of file.
- The conversation list and the push notification say *"Photo: …"* or *"File: …"*, so a phone that is not open still says what arrived.

**How the files are kept.** The bytes go to the company's own S3 folder under a new `chat/` area, one folder per conversation, and never into the database. **The bucket stays private.** No message carries a usable address: a link is asked for on the tap that wants the file, it is checked against the asker's membership of that conversation *at that moment*, and it stops working after five minutes. Somebody removed from a group stops being able to open its files from that moment, with nothing having to be moved.

**Refused before it is uploaded.** A file of the wrong kind or over the limit is refused in the browser and on the phone, by name and with the actual size, rather than after a 15 MB upload completes.

## Update / Modifications

### Fixed: the numbers on the app's dashboard

All four tiles on the app's dashboard were reading a payload shape the platform has never sent. Three of them silently showed **0**, and the fourth printed `[object Object]` where a count belonged, because it rendered an object instead of a number.

They now read the real figures — new leads, follow-ups due today, converted, and total clients — and each one goes through a guard that shows `0` only when the platform genuinely sends nothing, rather than when the field is simply named something else.

### Fixed: "Add user" could never be used by the person meant to use it

A pre-existing problem, found while building the above and worth stating plainly.

The users list fetched the company's roles from `/co/roles`, which requires **Role Management › Roles** permission. Somebody granted **Role Management › Users** but not *Roles* — which is the ordinary way to let an office manager add staff without letting them rewrite permissions — got nothing back from it, so the role dropdown was empty and **"Add user" stayed disabled with no explanation**.

There is now a narrower endpoint that returns role *names only*, under the **Users** permission, exposing no permission grid. Both the web and the app use it. The web asks for it only when the wider call came back empty, so nothing changes for an administrator who has both.

### Note on what a customer can see

A customer who signs in can start a conversation with the staff the chat directory lists, and that directory shows **names and roles only** — a phone number or an e-mail address is never part of what chat sends, for staff or customers. If you would rather customers reached only specific people, say so and it can be scoped in a follow-up; it is a deliberate choice left as-is rather than changed without consent.

## Performance

- **The searchable dropdown waits 180 ms (web) / 200 ms (app) before asking**, so a six-letter name is one request and not six.
- **Every answer is cached for the session**, so backspacing to something already typed is instant and silent.
- **A late answer is discarded, not painted.** A reply that arrives after a newer query has been typed is dropped, which is what otherwise makes a type-ahead flicker between results on a slow connection.
- **Mapped names come with the users list**, resolved in one query, instead of one request per customer row.
- **Lookups are capped at 20 rows** — this feeds a box somebody is typing into, and a list longer than a screenful is no more useful than a short one.
- **Attachment bytes never pass through the database.** The upload streams to S3 and the message carries only a key.

## Logs

- Creating or changing a user is recorded as before, now including the type and the mapping.
- Every attachment creates a message row carrying who sent it, its name, size and type, and the conversation it went to.

## Verified

- `npx tsc --noEmit` clean on both the platform and the app.
- `npm test` — all 58 checks pass, including the revision markers.
- `npm run build` clean.
- `npm run verify:bundle` — Metro bundles the app exactly as Gradle does, confirming the new `expo-document-picker` dependency resolves. This is the check that would have caught the v1.8.12 `netinfo` failure before a build was ever started.

## Build repository

`mobile/` and `.github/` must be pushed to the build repository with this release, as always. **This release adds a native dependency** (`expo-document-picker`), so a stale `mobile/` would fail to bundle. The revision markers were bumped to `1.9.0` for exactly this reason — Super Admin → Mobile App Release will report the repository as behind until it is pushed.

releases.title: The Mobile App tab never worked — this is why
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.15 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

**Builds now work end to end.** A signed `.apk` is compiled, uploaded to the company's S3 folder, and the row reaches **Ready**.

## Fixes

- **`404 · Company not found` on Super Admin → Company → Mobile App.** This is the original bug, properly found at last. The tab was reported in v1.7.0 as a spinner that never stopped; that release made the failure visible and added a retry, but treated the symptom. The cause was underneath it all along.

  These routes are mounted at `/companies/:id`, and **an Express sub-router does not inherit its mount path's parameters unless it is created with `{ mergeParams: true }`**. It was not. So `req.params.id` was `undefined`, the company lookup matched nothing, and every request to the tab answered *"Company not found"* — first as an endless spinner, then as a 404 that made no sense next to a company page that had clearly loaded.

  **It has never worked**, since the tab was added in v1.5.0.

- **The DPDP tab had exactly the same bug.** It is mounted the same way and reads the same parameter. It had a fallback to `?companyId=`, which no screen passes, so it was equally broken — just not yet opened. Both routers now merge their parameters, and the dead fallback is gone rather than left to hide the next one.

## Verified

Three ways, because a fix for a bug that survived two releases deserves more than a glance:

- **The Express behaviour itself**, run rather than recalled: a plain sub-router reports `req.params.id` as `null`; with `mergeParams` it reports the real id.
- **Every router in the project mounted under a path parameter is now checked**, so a new one cannot repeat this.
- **The test was confirmed to fail** when the bug is put back, and pass when it is removed. A check that cannot fail is worth nothing.

`npm test` — 58 checks, all passing.

## What to do

Deploy. Nothing to configure, and the tab will show this company's builds, downloads and signing key straight away.

releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.14 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

**The bucket fix from v1.8.13 worked.** The destination is now correct — `s3://cvs-whd-v1-20261014/CVS/app/android/1.0.0.12/…` — and a signed `.apk` reached it. Only the credentials were missing.

## Fixes

- **`NoCredentialsError: Unable to locate credentials`.** The upload runs **on the GitHub runner**, so it uses `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from the **repository's** secrets. They are not set there. The platform's own AWS credentials are a different thing and cannot be reached from a GitHub runner.

- **This is now the first thing the build checks, not the last.** A new first step confirms the repository has `MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, and stops in about a second if any is missing — naming them, and saying where they go. Until now the build installed 1,181 packages, bundled the JavaScript and compiled the app for six minutes before finding out it had nowhere to put the result.

- **"Set up secrets in GitHub" now writes the AWS credentials too.** It already wrote `MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET` and `BUILD_TRIGGER_SECRET`; it now also sends `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `AWS_REGION` when the platform has them. Each is sealed to the repository's own public key before it leaves, as the others are.

  The panel says plainly which five it sends, because credentials moving from one place to another should never be a surprise. If you would rather add them by hand, nothing has changed — the button is a convenience, not the only route.

## What to do

Either press **Set up secrets in GitHub** on *Mobile App Release*, or add these two in GitHub → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

| Secret | Value |
| --- | --- |

releases.title: Silent failures, and a typecheck that was never running
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.13 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## On the build log

The 123 lines from that run are **41 warnings and no errors**. They are Hermes compiler notes about JavaScript globals — `setTimeout`, `fetch`, `document`, `WebSocket`, `jest` — used without declaration, every one of them from inside a library: React Native's own polyfills, React's scheduler, `react-native-reanimated`, `get-intrinsic`, `pusher-js`. None come from this project's code, none can be fixed from here, and every React Native app produces them. The file they are reported against, `index.android.bundle`, only exists because bundling **succeeded**.

Two real bugs were found while checking, both mine, and both fixed below.

## Fixes

- **The mobile app was never actually typechecked.** `npx tsc --noEmit` in `mobile/` has been run before, but always without `node_modules` installed, so it failed on unresolved imports and never reached the code. Run properly for the first time, it found a genuine error: `src/lib/live.ts` loads pusher-js with a dynamic `import()`, and Expo's base config sets `target` but not `module`, leaving it at a level that predates dynamic import. **`module: ESNext` is now set**, and the app typechecks clean.

  A check that cannot run is worse than no check, because it reports success.

- **A screen whose data never arrived said nothing at all.** There are 63 places that load a screen with `api(...).then(setState)` and no `.catch`. If the call fails, the state is never set and the screen sits on a spinner with nothing to explain it — the same bug fixed on the Mobile App tab in v1.7.0, present on many other screens.

  The global handler that exists for exactly this **was skipping them on purpose**, with the comment *"API errors are already shown to the user as toasts"*. That is true of a call with a `.catch` — and those never reach a global handler. The ones that do are precisely the calls with no `.catch`, so the premise was backwards and the one thing that could have surfaced these was configured not to.

  An unhandled API failure now raises a toast saying what happened: *"You do not have permission for that."*, *"That was not found."*, or the platform's own message with *"Please try again."* One change, covering all 63 and anything added later.

## Verified

- **The mobile app bundles**: 1,219 modules, no errors, after the tsconfig change.
- **Both typechecks clean** — platform and app.
- **The silent failure is gone**, tested in a browser with every API call failing: Role Management now shows *"Database unreachable. Please try again."* where it used to spin with nothing on screen.
- `npm test` — 53 checks, all passing.

releases.title: The finished app had nowhere to go
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.12 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

**The app itself built.** A signed 66 MB `.apk` came out of that run — install, branding, prebuild, signing, JS bundling and all 34 Gradle tasks succeeded. Only the upload failed, and only because it had no bucket to upload to.

## Fixes

- **`upload failed: … to s3:///CVS/app/… Invalid bucket name ""`.** Three slashes: an empty bucket name. The upload runs **on the GitHub runner**, not on the platform, and the workflow read an `S3_BUCKET` **repository secret** — a second place to configure the same thing, which nobody had filled in because the platform's own `S3_BUCKET` was set and showing a green tick.

  **The platform now sends its bucket with every build**, inside the destination it already passes. There is no second place to configure, so the two can no longer disagree.

  A repository that still has an `S3_BUCKET` secret keeps working: the workflow uses the address the platform sends when it is a full `s3://` one, and falls back to the secret otherwise. And if there is no bucket either way, it now says so in one line — *"The app built fine — only the upload had nowhere to go."* — instead of printing an AWS regex.

- **"Check GitHub setup" now checks the repository's own secrets.** The runner reports back and uploads, so it needs `MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` of its own. The checklist listed the AWS pair as platform settings only, which is where the confusion came from. It now lists them for the repository too, and the live check names any that are absent.

## Verified

The address parsing is the whole fix, so it was run against every case rather than reasoned about: a full `s3://bucket/path` from the current platform, a deep path, a bare prefix with the old repository secret, no bucket anywhere (refused with the plain message), and a bucket with no path at all. That last one found a real bug before it shipped — `${REST#*/}` leaves the string untouched when there is no slash, which would have put the bucket name inside the key.

`npm test` — 53 checks, all passing.

## What to do

Push `.github/` and deploy the platform. Nothing to configure: the bucket comes from the platform's own `S3_BUCKET`, which is already set.

While you are in GitHub, check the repository has **`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`** and **`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`** as secrets — the upload needs them, and *Check GitHub setup* will now tell you if they are missing.

releases.title: The app bundles — a missing dependency, and a check that would have found it
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.11 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **`Unable to resolve module @react-native-community/netinfo` — `createBundleReleaseJsAndAssets` FAILED.** Chat connects through `pusher-js/react-native`, and that build of pusher-js requires `@react-native-community/netinfo` internally. I added pusher-js in v1.6.0 without it.

  It is now a dependency of the app, at **11.3.1**, the version Expo SDK 51 pins. The lockfile is regenerated.

  **Why nothing caught this earlier.** pusher-js does not declare netinfo as a peer dependency — it simply requires it inside its React Native build — so `npm` never warned, and a sweep of our own imports never saw it either, because none of our code imports it. **Only bundling the app finds it**, which is why Gradle was the first thing to notice, four and a half minutes into a build.

## New

- **`npm run verify:bundle`** installs the app's dependencies and runs Metro exactly as Gradle's bundle step does. It takes about forty seconds and catches this entire class of failure — a missing or broken module — before a build is ever started. **This release was verified with it: 1,219 modules, a 3.26 MB bundle, no errors.**

- **The platform now checks the app source as well as the workflow.** v1.8.11 taught *Check GitHub setup* to notice a stale `.github/`; it now does the same for `mobile/`, which is the other half of the same problem:

  - *"mobile/ is revision 1.8.12 — current."*
  - *"mobile/ on main is revision 1.8.0; this platform ships 1.8.12. Push the mobile folder from the current release."*

  Pushing one half without the other was going to keep costing a build at a time.

## What to do

Push **both** `.github/` and `mobile/` to your build repository, then build.

`mobile/package-lock.json` is part of this — it is how the build installs exactly these versions, and it is what carries netinfo.

releases.title: The platform now notices when the repository is running an old workflow
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.10 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## The problem this solves

Every release has **two halves that deploy separately**:

| Half | Where it goes | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The platform | Vercel | Deploy |
| `.github/` and `mobile/` | Your build repository | **Commit and push** |

Deploying the platform does **not** change the workflow GitHub runs. So a build can keep failing on something that was fixed two releases ago, with nothing on screen to suggest why — the panel is reading the platform's own settings, while GitHub is running a file from last week.

## Fixes

- **The workflow now carries a revision**, `# lms-workflow:`, and the platform knows which one it expects. **Check GitHub setup** reads the file in your repository and compares, so *Workflow file* now says one of:

  - *"…is on main, revision 1.8.11 — current."*
  - *"…on main is revision 1.8.0; this platform ships 1.8.11. Push the .github folder from the current release."*
  - *"…is on main, but it is an older copy from before the revisions were marked."*

  The revision only changes when the workflow or one of its scripts actually changes, so it does not cry wolf on every release.

- **A test keeps the two honest.** `npm test` fails if the marker in the workflow and the constant in the platform ever disagree — a check that lies is worse than no check.

## If you are seeing `python3: can't open file …android-signing-config.py`

That message can only come from the **old** workflow. The word `python3` does not appear anywhere in v1.8.10 or later. Push `.github/` to your build repository and the error goes with it.

Delete the two `.py` files while you are there — they were replaced by `.mjs` in v1.8.10 and will otherwise sit in the repository doing nothing.

releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.9 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **`can't open file '…/mobile/.github/scripts/android-signing-config.py'`.** The build job sets `working-directory: mobile`, so every step runs from the app's own folder. Two steps called scripts as `.github/scripts/…`, which from there means `mobile/.github/scripts/…` — a folder that does not exist. The three `report.mjs` steps had `working-directory: .` and were right; these two never did.

  Both now call `../.github/scripts/…`, reaching the repository root from the job's own directory.

  This failed **after** signing succeeded, which is worth noting: the keystore work from v1.8.9 did run, and ran correctly.

## Updates / Modifications

- **The two Python scripts are now Node**, to match the stack: Next.js and Node on the platform, React Native on the phone, nothing else.

  - `android-signing-config.py` → **`android-signing-config.mjs`**. Same job, same output.
  - `play-upload.py` → **`play-upload.mjs`**, and it no longer installs anything. It talks to Google's Publishing API over plain HTTPS: a service-account JWT signed with Node's own crypto, exchanged for an access token, then four REST calls. No SDK, no `pip install`, nothing between the key and Google.

  The `python3 -m pip install` line is gone with them, which also takes a slow step out of every store build.

## Verified

`npm test` — seventeen new checks beside the existing ones, none needing a runner:

- the workflow runs **no Python at all**, and every script it names is Node;
- **every script path resolves to a file that exists**, from the directory that step actually runs in — the exact bug above;
- the signing-config rewrite adds the release config, points the release build at it, leaves the debug build and the existing debug keystore alone, and changes nothing when run twice (prebuild can run more than once, and so can it).

## What to do

Push `.github/` and build again. The two `.py` files are deleted — remove them from your repository too, or they will sit there doing nothing.

releases.title: The signing key is made in JavaScript, because the platform has no JDK
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.8 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **`Could not make the signing key: spawn keytool ENOENT`.** The platform-held signing key, added in v1.7.0, was made by shelling out to **`keytool`** — a program that belongs to the JDK. The platform runs on a Node runtime, which has no JDK and never will. So the very first Android build of every company failed, and no setting could have fixed it. That was a design error on my part, not a configuration problem: I reached for the tool I would have used at a terminal without asking whether the server had it.

  **The keystore is now built in JavaScript**, with `node-forge`: an RSA-2048 key, a self-signed certificate valid for 10,000 days, and a PKCS#12 keystore — the same artefact `keytool -storetype PKCS12` produced, and exactly what Gradle reads.

- **One password, not two.** The old code made separate store and key passwords. PKCS#12 keeps one, and Java refuses a keystore where they differ — so that first build would have failed again even with a JDK present.

- **The fingerprint is now the certificate's.** It is the SHA-256 of the certificate, which is what Play Console shows and what an installed phone compares. The old code fell back to hashing the keystore file, a number that matches nothing.

- **Making a key no longer blocks the server.** RSA generation ran synchronously and held the event loop for several seconds, so one company's first build made every other request wait. It now yields between rounds.

## Verified

Against a real JDK, once, which is the only way to be sure:

- **`keytool -list -v`** reads the keystore and reports `Entry type: PrivateKeyEntry`, the right alias, `SHA256withRSA`, validity to 2054, and **the same SHA-256 fingerprint** the platform recorded.
- **`jarsigner`** signs with it, and `jarsigner -verify` answers **"jar verified"**. (It warns the certificate is self-signed, which is correct — every Android app signing certificate is.)

And on every run, with no JDK needed: `npm test` now includes eleven checks that the keystore opens with its password and not another, holds exactly one usable private key under the company's alias, carries a self-signed certificate lasting well past 25 years, produces a real SHA-256 fingerprint, and gives every company a different key.

## What to do

Deploy and build again. `MOBILE_SIGNING_SECRET` is already set, and nothing else is needed — the first Android build of each company now makes that company's permanent key and signs with it.

**The failed builds in the table can be left alone.** No key was stored, so nothing is half-made; the next build starts clean.

- **A build with no signing key ran for ten minutes before saying so.** An Android app has to be signed, and there are two ways to do it: `MOBILE_SIGNING_SECRET` on the platform, or the four `ANDROID_*` secrets in the build repository. With neither, the build installed every dependency, branded itself, ran prebuild, and *then* failed at the signing step.

  The platform could have known. It can already read which secrets a repository holds — that is how *"Set up secrets in GitHub"* works — so it now checks before dispatching and refuses in about a second, naming which secrets are missing and both ways to fix it.

- **"Check GitHub setup" has a fifth answer: Signing.** It says which of the two routes is in use, or that neither is, before anybody presses Build.

- **The `MOBILE_SIGNING_SECRET` row no longer says "optional" without saying what it costs.** It now reads: one of these two is required for Android; with neither, an Android build fails at the signing step.

- **Not being able to check never blocks a build.** If GitHub cannot be reached, or the token cannot read secrets, the answer is "unverified" and the build goes ahead — the build itself still refuses to produce an unsigned app. Refusing a build because we could not check would be worse than letting it report the truth.

## Why the platform does not simply make this one up

`MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET` is now made and kept by the platform (v1.8.1), and the obvious question is why `MOBILE_SIGNING_SECRET` is not.

They are not the same kind of secret. The build secret signs messages in flight. **The signing secret is what encrypts every company's Android keystore at rest**, and its whole purpose is that the database on its own cannot sign anything. Generating it and storing it in that same database would keep the ceremony and throw away the point.

So it stays a platform setting. It is **one value, set once, for every company for ever** — and then the platform makes, keeps and uses a permanent key per company with nothing further to do.

## What to do

```
openssl rand -hex 32
```

Add it as **`MOBILE_SIGNING_SECRET`** in the platform's environment (Vercel → Settings → Environment Variables → Production), redeploy, and build again. Nothing else — no keystore, no `keytool`, no `ANDROID_*` secrets.

**Keep that value.** It is the only thing that can decrypt the signing keys. Lose it and no existing app can ever be updated again; every phone needs an uninstall and reinstall.

releases.title: Uploads now say what went wrong
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.6 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **Uploading a branding image showed an error that explained nothing.** The error handler turned **any** error that was not one of ours into *"Internal server error (ref …)"*. Two ordinary, fixable things landed there:

  1. **An image over the size limit.** The limit was **3 MB**, which an ordinary side banner exceeds without trying. The upload was refused by `multer` before it reached any of our code, so nobody was told the size was the problem.
  2. **Any refusal from S3** — wrong bucket name, missing permission, an expired key — came back the same way, with the actual reason only in a server log.

- **Both now say what to do**, translated once in the error handler so every upload in the platform benefits — branding, knowledge base, DPDP documents, notification sounds, client attachments:

  | What happened | What you now see |
  | --- | --- |
  | Image too big | *"That file is too large. The most this accepts is 8 MB — save it smaller and try again."* |
  | Bucket wrong | *"File storage: The S3 bucket named in S3_BUCKET does not exist. Check the name and the region."* |
  | No permission | *"File storage: S3 refused the write. The access key needs s3:PutObject on this bucket and prefix."* |
  | Key wrong | *"File storage: S3 does not recognise AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID."* |
  | Secret wrong | *"File storage: S3 rejected the signature — AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY does not match the key id."* |

  A genuine fault is still a 500 with a reference number and still keeps its message off the screen. That has not changed.

- **The branding image limit is now 8 MB**, up from 3 MB. The company-logo upload on the company form was 2 MB and now matches.

- **The browser refuses an impossible image immediately.** Picking one that is too large, or not an image type the platform accepts, says so the moment it is chosen — rather than after it has been uploaded and rejected.

- **An image that fails now says which one.** Three images are uploaded in a row after the company's details are saved; a failure used to give one message with no indication of which. It now names the image — and makes clear the details themselves were saved, because they were.

## Verified

Twelve cases, no database needed: `npm test`.

- every `multer` limit and every S3 refusal maps to its own sentence, with the right status;
- our own errors, duplicate keys and genuine crashes all behave exactly as before;
- a genuine crash still does not leak its message to the browser.

releases.title: The app images the build needs are now in the repository
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.5 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **`ENOENT: no such file or directory, open './assets/icon.png'` — Prebuild failed.** `mobile/assets/` was an empty folder. It has been empty since v1.5.0: `app.json` named four images, the folder was created, and the images themselves were never put in it. Expo's prebuild reads the icon to make every Android density, so it died before the app was compiled — with an ENOENT stack trace from inside `@expo/image-utils` that says nothing about what to do.

  **Four images are now committed in `mobile/assets/`:**

  | File | Size | What it is |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `icon.png` | 1024² | The full-bleed icon, for iOS and both store listings |
  | `adaptive-icon.png` | 1024² | The Android adaptive foreground, with the mark inside the safe area so a circular or squircle mask does not cut it |
  | `splash.png` | 1242² | Shown over the splash colour, which is set to the company's own |
  | `notification-icon.png` | 96² | The small monochrome mark Android draws in the status bar |

  The mark is a hive cell in the platform's green and honey — deliberate rather than placeholder, and tied to no particular industry.

- **A company's own icon still wins.** When one has been uploaded, the build downloads it and it replaces both icon shapes, as before. The log now says which of the two happened, instead of being silent when it used the default.

- **A missing image now fails with a sentence, not a stack trace.** `brand.mjs` checks all four exist before prebuild runs and names any that do not, with where they should be.

## Updates / Modifications

- **`app.json` now points the Android adaptive icon and the notification icon at their own images**, rather than reusing the full-bleed one for all three. Android masks the adaptive foreground, so a full-bleed image loses its edges; and the status-bar mark has to be a flat silhouette or Android draws a grey square.

## What to do

**Push the `mobile/` folder** — the new part is `mobile/assets/` and the updated `app.json` and `scripts/brand.mjs`. Then build again.

**To give a company its own icon:** upload one under that company's Branding, and the next build uses it. Upload it already padded if you care how it looks under Android's circular mask, since the same image is used for both shapes.

releases.title: The app now has a lockfile, and caching can no longer fail a build
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.4 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed. This release fixes the first real build failure on GitHub — the workflow now dispatches and runs, which it never did before v1.8.4.

## Fixes

- **`Error: Some specified paths were not resolved, unable to cache dependencies.`** The workflow asked `actions/setup-node` to cache npm packages keyed on `mobile/package-lock.json`, and that file had never been committed. `setup-node` does not treat a missing cache path as "skip the cache" — it fails the step outright, which failed the build before a single line of the app was compiled.

  Two things were wrong, and both are fixed:

  1. **`mobile/package-lock.json` is now in the repository.** All 17 dependencies resolved, 1,188 packages, `lockfileVersion 3`. This is worth having for its own sake: `npm ci` installs exactly these versions every time, so two builds of the same company's app a month apart produce the same thing. Without it, `npm install` was free to pick up a newer patch release of any dependency mid-build.
  2. **Caching is now switched on only when the lockfile is there** — `cache: ${{ hashFiles(...) != '' && 'npm' || '' }}`. A missing lockfile now means "no cache", not "no build".

- **The Install step says which way it went.** With a lockfile it runs `npm ci` (falling back to `npm install` if the lockfile and `package.json` have drifted apart); without one it runs `npm install` and leaves a warning in the log saying the build may not match the last one.

## What to do

**Push the updated `mobile/` folder**, including the new `mobile/package-lock.json`, along with `.github/workflows/build-mobile.yml`. Then start the build again.

## A note on where this sits

The workflow reaching `setup-node` at all means the platform side is now correct end to end: the build dispatched, GitHub accepted it, the runner started and checked the code out. What remains are the ordinary problems of building a React Native app in CI, which fail loudly in the run log with the compiler's own words.

releases.title: This platform builds mobile apps, and no longer offers to build something else
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.3 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **`GITHUB_BUILD_WORKFLOW` is no longer read.** It was a setting with exactly one correct value and one very easy wrong one.

  The sibling restaurant platform has a variable of the same name naming a **desktop installer** workflow. Environment files get copied between projects, so `build-desktop.yml` arrived here and pointed a mobile platform at a workflow that does not exist in this repository. Every build answered **404**, and because of the bug fixed in v1.8.3, that 404 arrived as *"Internal server error (ref …)"*.

  This platform ships exactly one workflow and builds mobile apps. There was never anything to choose, so it no longer offers a choice: **`.github/workflows/build-mobile.yml` is a constant.**

- **A leftover value is reported, not obeyed.** If `GITHUB_BUILD_WORKFLOW` is still set to anything else, both set-up panels say *"…is ignored — this platform builds mobile apps with build-mobile.yml. You can delete that variable."* Nothing breaks while it sits there; it simply does nothing.

- **The row is gone from the set-up checklist**, because a setting that is not read has no business being on a list of things to set.

## What this means for you

**Nothing to do.** You do not have to change `GITHUB_BUILD_WORKFLOW` — it is ignored either way. Deleting it just tidies up.

If you have already pushed `.github/workflows/build-mobile.yml` to your branch and opened the repository's Actions tab once, a build should now dispatch. **Check GitHub setup** will confirm all four answers before you press Build.

## A note on the one thing a rename costs

Renaming the workflow file in your repository is no longer supported — the platform asks GitHub for `build-mobile.yml` by name. That is a deliberate trade: one genuinely rare need, against a wrong value that arrives for free every time an environment file is copied from another project.

releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.2 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed.

## Fixes

- **"Internal server error (ref …)" when starting a build from Mobile App Release.** `startBuild()` explains itself — *"GitHub refused the build (404)…"*, *"Switch on S3 storage for this company…"*, *"An Android build is already running…"* — and the release console let every one of those escape as an unhandled exception, which the error handler turned into an opaque reference number. The company's own Mobile App tab had caught them correctly since v1.5.0; this route never did. **The real reason is now shown.**

  In the case reported, the message underneath was almost certainly *"GitHub refused the build (404). Push .github/workflows/build-mobile.yml to the branch and open the Actions tab once so Actions are enabled."* — because `GITHUB_BUILD_WORKFLOW` is still set to `build-desktop.yml`, which belongs to another project and does not exist in this repository.

## New Features

- **"Check GitHub setup" now actually asks GitHub.** It used to re-read this platform's own settings, which can only ever tell you a value is present and well-formed — never whether it is *true*. It now asks four questions and gives four plain answers, each with what to do:

  | | |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Repository** | Can the token see `owner/repo` at all? Separates "does not exist", "no access" and "token expired". |
  | **Branch** | Does the branch being built from exist? Names the default if not. |
  | **Workflow file** | Is `.github/workflows/<name>` actually **on that branch**? This is the one that bites. |
  | **Actions** | Has GitHub registered the workflow? It does not until Actions has been opened once. |

  Every answer that is wrong carries the fix, not just the complaint.

- **A workflow name from another project is now flagged.** The platform ships exactly one workflow, `build-mobile.yml`, so anything else gets an amber note — and where the name contains "desktop" it says plainly that it is another project's and will not build an app. **It does not block the build**, because renaming a file on purpose is legitimate; *Check GitHub setup* is what settles it.

- **`BuildRequirement.warn`** is new, beside `check`: a value that is not broken but is probably not what was meant. A `check` blocks, a `warn` does not. Existing requirements are unaffected.

## What to do with this release

1. Set **`GITHUB_BUILD_WORKFLOW=build-mobile.yml`**, or remove the variable entirely — that is already the default.
2. Make sure `.github/workflows/build-mobile.yml` is **committed and pushed** to the branch you build from. It is in the release zip, inside the hidden `.github` folder (`Cmd ⇧ .` on macOS, View → Hidden items on Windows).
3. Open the repository's **Actions** tab once. GitHub does not register a workflow until somebody has.
4. Press **Check GitHub setup**. It will tell you which of those four is still wrong, if any.

releases.title: Builds were refused for a setting that is deliberately empty
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.1 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed. Two bugs are fixed, both of which stopped a build starting.

## Fixes

- **A build was refused for `MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET` even though the platform keeps one.** This is a regression from v1.8.1. That release taught the set-up panel that a secret kept by the platform is not a missing one, by giving `readyToBuild()` a map of what the platform holds — but `startBuild()` still called `readyToBuild()` with nothing. So the panel showed a green tick and an enabled button, and the build itself answered *"Not set up yet — missing MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET"*. The gate is now given the same knowledge the panel has, and the secret is made **before** the gate is checked rather than after, since it is one of the things the gate looks for.

  The general lesson is in the code as a comment: when the thing that decides and the thing that displays are told different stories, only one of them is on screen.

- **"Every company that already has an app (0)" could be ticked, and did nothing.** Nobody can have an app before the first one is built, so with a count of zero that option is a guaranteed no-op — and it answered *"0 builds started"*, which says what happened and not one word about why. Now:
  - it cannot be ticked while the count is zero, and unticks itself if the count falls to zero;
  - the reason sits under it: *"No company has an app yet, so there is nothing to rebuild. Pick a company above and build its first one."*;
  - **Start build** is disabled rather than pressable-but-pointless;
  - if the request is made anyway, the platform refuses it with that reason instead of a silent zero;
  - a bulk build that starts nothing for some other reason now reports the first actual problem rather than a bare count.

- **A first build says so.** Building a company that has no app reports *"First build started — it takes 10–20 minutes and fixes this company's application id."*, because that build decides something permanent.

## Verified

The gate logic is covered by a test of all eight cases — with and without the platform-held secret, an environment-set secret, a too-short one, a `https://…​.git` repository and a workflow without `.yml`. All pass. It needs no database, so it runs anywhere.

## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.8.0 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed. This release stops asking you for a setting the platform can make itself, and closes a hole in how that setting behaved when it was missing.

## Fixes

- **A missing `MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET` used to fail open.** The platform signed with the literal string `"dev"` (`env("MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET") || "dev"`) — a value printed in the source — so an unconfigured platform accepted any build result signed with that known string. `/api/public/mobile/build` decides which file a company installs as its app, and since v1.7.0 the same secret guards the endpoint that hands over a company's Android keystore. **With no secret, both now refuse.** The platform makes one on its own, so there is no longer any reason for it to be missing.

## Updates / Modifications

- **`MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET` is no longer an environment variable you have to invent.** The platform makes one the first time it is needed, keeps it, and shows it on the set-up panel to copy — exactly as `BUILD_TRIGGER_SECRET` has always worked. **An environment variable still wins where one is set**, so a platform already configured behaves exactly as before and the panel says which of the two is in use.
- **"Set up secrets in GitHub"** writes both shared secrets into the build repository over the GitHub API, so there is nothing to paste. GitHub will not accept a secret in the clear, so each value is sealed to the repository's own public key (libsodium sealed box) before it is sent.
  - It needs the build token to carry **Secrets: read and write** as well as Actions. Where it does not, the refusal is reported for each secret on its own and the values are still shown to copy — **the manual route never stops working**.
  - Each secret's outcome is reported separately, because "two of three worked" is the thing worth knowing.
- **A new callback secret can be made from the panel.** Everything building at that moment will fail to report back, which the screen says before it is pressed. A secret that came from the environment cannot be replaced from here — it says where to change it instead.
- **The set-up checklist understands what the platform keeps.** A row the platform holds is a tick with its own line — *"Kept by the platform — nothing to set here"* — not a red cross for a variable that is deliberately absent.
- **`setupState()` and `readyToBuild()` take an optional map** of what the platform holds. Called with nothing, both behave exactly as they did in v1.7.1.
- **`callbackValid()` is now async**, because it reads a stored secret. Both callers await it.

## What this means for you

If you have already set `MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET` in the environment: **nothing changes.** It still wins, and the panel says so.

If you have not: stop. Open **Super Admin → Mobile App Release → Set up in GitHub**, and either press **Set up secrets in GitHub**, or press **Show** and copy both values into the repository's secrets by hand. Nothing goes in the environment.

**One behaviour genuinely changes at deploy:** a platform that today has no secret set is silently signing with `"dev"`. After this it refuses until a secret exists — which is the point — so any build in flight at deploy time will fail to report back and need starting again.

releases.title: Publishing to Google Play and the App Store
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.7.1 is unchanged. Every existing build keeps working exactly as it did: with nothing new configured, pressing Build still produces the `.apk` and ad-hoc `.ipa` it always has, in the same place, on the same download page. Nothing was removed.

## New Features

- **Store build.** A build is now either:
  - **Direct install** — the `.apk` and ad-hoc `.ipa` you have always had, and still the default; or
  - **Store upload** — an **`.aab`** for Google Play and an **App Store `.ipa`** for App Store Connect, which are the only formats the two stores accept.

  Choose it with **Store build** on the company's Mobile App tab, or **What it is for** on *Mobile App Release*. Both screens say in one line what file you are about to get, before you press the button — an `.aab` handed to someone expecting to install it wastes an afternoon.
- **It uploads itself, if you let it.** With the store credentials in the build repository, a store build goes straight to Google Play's **Internal testing** track and to **TestFlight**. Without them the file is still built and kept in the company's folder, and the build row says *"kept on S3 — add … to upload automatically"*. Either way works; neither is a lesser path.
- **The result is recorded on the build**, so the builds table says *"uploaded to the Internal testing track (version code 14)"* or exactly why a store refused it — unknown application id, missing permission, a build number already used.
- **A failed upload never fails the build.** The file is already stored before the upload is attempted, so a store being unreachable costs a retry, not a rebuild.
- **Store builds are kept off the company's download page.** An `.aab` cannot install on a phone, so offering one would hand somebody a file that cannot work and no way to find out why. Super Admin still sees every build.
- **A new guide**, *Knowledge Base › Publishing to Google Play and the App Store*: the one-time set-up in each store, what to paste where, and what each refusal actually means.

## Updates / Modifications

- **Nothing can reach the public on its own.** The Play upload goes to **Internal testing** and the Apple upload to **TestFlight**. Promoting to Production, or submitting for review, stays a decision somebody makes in the Play Console or App Store Connect. This is deliberate.
- **The workflow gained one input, `target`**, which decides `assembleRelease` versus `bundleRelease` on Android and which export options are used on iOS. An older dispatch without it behaves exactly as before, because it defaults to `test`.
- **New export options file** `.github/ios-export-store.plist` (`method: app-store`). The existing `ios-export.plist` is untouched and still used for direct installs. **Note:** a store build needs an **App Store** provisioning profile in `IOS_PROFILE_BASE64`; an ad-hoc profile builds fine and is then refused on upload.
- **`MobileBuild` gained `target` and `store`** (uploaded, track, at, message). Existing rows have no value in them and are treated as direct installs, which is what they were.
- **Three new repository secrets, all optional** — add them only if you want the upload to happen by itself:

  | Secret | For |
  | --- | --- |
  | `GOOGLE_PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON` | Google Play |
  | `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID`, `APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID`, `APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_P8` | App Store Connect |

  They are checked by the build itself, like the other repository secrets, and appear on the set-up panel as optional.
- **The Play upload talks to Google's own Publishing API** from `.github/scripts/play-upload.py` — no third-party action ever sees the service-account key or the bundle.
- **`latestReady()` takes a second argument**, `onlyInstallable`. The company's own page passes it; the Super Admin screens do not. Every existing caller keeps its previous behaviour.

## Before the first store build

1. **Create the app in each store** with exactly the application id / bundle id the Build screen shows, and upload one build by hand. Neither store accepts an unknown id over an API, so the first one always goes through the console.
2. **Then add the secrets above**, if you want it automatic.
3. The guide walks through both, including what each refusal means.

## Next

v1.9.0 — a build history page on the company side, attachments in chat, and release notes shown to each company inside its own app.

releases.title: The set-up checker now catches what it used to wave through
releases.md:
## AS-IS

Everything from v1.0.0 to v1.7.0 is unchanged. No screen, field or behaviour was removed. This release only makes the build set-up panel tell the truth about three settings it used to pass silently.

## Updates / Modifications

- **A setting that is present but unusable is no longer a green tick.** The checker only ever asked "is there a value?", so a wrong one passed and the build then failed on GitHub with a 404 and nothing useful to show for it. Three are now checked properly, and a bad one shows in amber with the correction rather than the complaint:
  - **`GITHUB_BUILD_REPO`** must be `owner/repo`. A full `https://github.com/owner/repo.git` is pasted straight into a GitHub address and cannot work — and when that is what it finds, the message names the short form to use.
  - **`GITHUB_BUILD_WORKFLOW`** must end in `.yml`. Another project's desktop workflow will not build an app.
  - **`MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET`** must be long enough to be a secret, with the command to make one.
- **A malformed setting also blocks the build**, the same as a missing one. Starting a build that is going to fail a minute later on GitHub helps nobody.
- **`MOBILE_SIGNING_SECRET` is now on the checklist, and clearly marked optional.** It was added in v1.7.0 and documented everywhere except the one screen whose job is to show what is missing. It is also worded properly now: leaving it empty and keeping the `ANDROID_*` secrets in the repository is **a complete set-up on its own**, not a lesser one.
- **`MOBILE_BUILD_SECRET`'s description now says what happens if the two values differ** — builds run but never turn Ready — because that is the symptom people actually meet.

## Fixes

- **`.github/workflows/build-mobile.yml` was not valid YAML.** The signing step contained a Python heredoc whose lines de-indented below the block they sat in, which ends the block early. GitHub would have rejected the whole file with *"Invalid workflow file"* on the first run. The Python now lives in `.github/scripts/android-signing-config.py` and the workflow calls it, which also means that script can be read and tested on its own. **This has been broken since v1.5.0** and nothing that depends on it has ever run.
